summary.text: First derive the Euclid–Euler form \(n=2^kq\), where \(q=2^{k+1}-1\) is prime, and use the proper divisors \(1,2,\ldots,2^k\) together with \(q,2q,\ldots,2^{k-1}q\): binary expansions of the quotient and remainder modulo \(q\) represent every integer from \(0\) to \(n\) as a subset sum (with \(n=(2^k-1)q+q\) handling the endpoint). Since perfection makes the sum of all proper divisors equal to \(n\), no subset sum exceeds \(n\), so the distinct sums are exactly \(0,1,\ldots,n\), and removing the empty sum leaves \(n\) values.

full_proof.text:
Let \(D(n)\) denote the set of positive proper divisors of \(n\), and let
\[
\mathcal S(n)=\left\{\sum_{d\in T}d:T\subseteq D(n)\right\}.
\]
The empty subset is allowed in \(\mathcal S(n)\), so \(0\in\mathcal S(n)\). By definition,
\[
a(n)=|\mathcal S(n)|-1.
\]
We prove that if \(n\) is even and perfect, then
\[
\mathcal S(n)=\{0,1,\ldots,n\}.
\]
It will then follow immediately that \(|\mathcal S(n)|=n+1\), and hence \(a(n)=n\).

We first derive the needed form of an even perfect number.

### 1. The form of an even perfect number

Write
\[
M_t=2^t-1
\]
for the \(t\)-th Mersenne number. We will show that an even perfect number \(n\) can be written
\[
n=2^kM_{k+1}=2^k(2^{k+1}-1),
\]
where \(M_{k+1}\) is prime.

Because a perfect number is positive, we may factor out the largest power of \(2\) dividing \(n\). Thus there are natural numbers \(k,m\) such that
\[
n=2^k m
\]
and \(m\) is odd. Equivalently, \(2^k\) and \(m\) are coprime.

Let \(\sigma(x)\) be the sum of all positive divisors of \(x\). Since \(2^k\) and \(m\) are coprime, multiplicativity of the divisor-sum function gives
\[
\sigma(n)=\sigma(2^k)\sigma(m).
\]
The divisors of \(2^k\) are \(1,2,\ldots,2^k\), so the geometric-series identity gives
\[
\sigma(2^k)=1+2+\cdots+2^k=2^{k+1}-1=M_{k+1}.
\]
On the other hand, because \(n\) is perfect, its proper divisors sum to \(n\); adding \(n\) itself shows that
\[
\sigma(n)=2n=2^{k+1}m.
\]
Consequently,
\[
M_{k+1}\sigma(m)=2^{k+1}m. \tag{1}
\]

The number \(M_{k+1}=2^{k+1}-1\) is odd, and therefore it is coprime to \(2^{k+1}\). Equation (1) shows that \(M_{k+1}\) divides \(2^{k+1}m\). Euclid's lemma therefore implies that \(M_{k+1}\mid m\). Write
\[
m=M_{k+1}j
\]
for some natural number \(j\). Since \(m>0\), we have \(j>0\). Substituting this into (1) and cancelling the positive factor \(M_{k+1}\), we obtain
\[
\sigma(M_{k+1}j)=2^{k+1}j=(M_{k+1}+1)j=M_{k+1}j+j. \tag{2}
\]

For a positive integer \(x\), the sum of all divisors is the sum of its proper divisors plus \(x\). Thus, if \(P(x)\) denotes the sum of the proper divisors of \(x\), equation (2) says
\[
P(M_{k+1}j)+M_{k+1}j=M_{k+1}j+j,
\]
and cancellation gives
\[
P(M_{k+1}j)=j. \tag{3}
\]
In particular, \(P(M_{k+1}j)=j\) divides \(M_{k+1}j\).

We use the following elementary observation: if the sum \(P(x)\) of the proper divisors of a positive integer \(x\) divides \(x\), then
\[
P(x)=1\quad\text{or}\quad P(x)=x.
\]
To see this, a divisor of \(x\) cannot exceed \(x\). If \(P(x)<x\), then \(P(x)\) itself is a proper divisor of \(x\). If it were greater than \(1\), then both \(1\) and \(P(x)\) would be distinct proper divisors, so the sum of all proper divisors would be at least \(1+P(x)>P(x)\), a contradiction. Hence in the strict case \(P(x)=1\); the only other possibility is \(P(x)=x\).

Apply this observation to \(x=M_{k+1}j\). There are two cases.

First, suppose
\[
P(M_{k+1}j)=1.
\]
By (3), \(j=1\), and hence
\[
P(M_{k+1})=1.
\]
A positive integer has sum of proper divisors equal to \(1\) exactly when it is prime: a prime has only the proper divisor \(1\), while a composite integer greater than \(1\) has at least one further proper divisor and therefore has proper-divisor sum greater than \(1\). Thus \(M_{k+1}\) is prime. Since \(m=M_{k+1}j\), we have \(m=M_{k+1}\), and therefore
\[
n=2^kM_{k+1}.
\]

Second, suppose
\[
P(M_{k+1}j)=M_{k+1}j.
\]
Together with (3), this gives
\[
j=M_{k+1}j.
\]
Since \(j>0\), cancellation yields \(M_{k+1}=1\). If \(k\ge 1\), then
\[
M_{k+1}=2^{k+1}-1\ge 3,
\]
a contradiction. If \(k=0\), then \(n=m\), which is odd by the choice of \(m\), contradicting the hypothesis that \(n\) is even. Thus this second case is impossible.

We have proved that there is a natural number \(k\) for which
\[
q:=M_{k+1}=2^{k+1}-1
\]
is prime and
\[
n=2^kq. \tag{4}
\]
Moreover \(k>0\): if \(k=0\), then \(q=M_1=1\) and (4) would give \(n=1\), which is not even.

### 2. Binary subset sums

We next record the standard binary subset-sum fact. For every natural number \(p\), every integer \(u\) satisfying
\[
0\le u<2^p
\]
can be expressed as a sum of distinct members of
\[
\{1,2,4,\ldots,2^{p-1}\}.
\]

This can be proved by induction on \(p\). For \(p=0\), the inequality \(u<1\) forces \(u=0\), represented by the empty subset. Suppose the assertion holds for \(p\), and let \(u<2^{p+1}=2^p+2^p\). If \(u<2^p\), use the induction hypothesis without choosing \(2^p\). Otherwise, \(0\le u-2^p<2^p\); represent \(u-2^p\) using distinct powers \(1,2,\ldots,2^{p-1}\), and then add \(2^p\). Since all the earlier powers are strictly smaller than \(2^p\), this addition preserves distinctness. This proves the assertion.

### 3. Two families of proper divisors

Retain the notation
\[
q=2^{k+1}-1,
\qquad n=2^kq,
\qquad k>0.
\]
Since \(q\) is prime, in particular \(q>1\). Consider the following two finite sets:
\[
A=\{2^i:0\le i\le k\}

a\quad\text{and}\quad
B=\{2^iq:0\le i<k\}.
\]
Every member of \(A\cup B\) is a proper divisor of \(n\).

Indeed, if \(0\le i\le k\), then \(2^i\mid 2^k\mid n\), and
\[
2^i\le 2^k<2^kq=n
\]
because \(q>1\). Hence \(2^i\) is a proper divisor of \(n\).

Likewise, if \(0\le i<k\), then \(2^iq\mid 2^kq=n\), and
\[
2^iq<2^kq=n,
\]
so \(2^iq\) is also a proper divisor.

The sets \(A\) and \(B\) are disjoint. Every member of \(A\) is at most \(2^k\), whereas every member of \(B\) is at least \(q\). Since \(k>0\),
\[
q=2^{k+1}-1=2\cdot 2^k-1>2^k.
\]
Thus every member of \(A\) is strictly smaller than every member of \(B\).

### 4. Representing every integer from \(0\) to \(n\)

We now show that every integer \(m\) with
\[
0\le m\le n=2^kq
\]
is the sum of a subset of \(A\cup B\), and therefore is a sum of distinct proper divisors of \(n\).

There is a small special case at the upper endpoint. Define integers \(d,r\) as follows:

- if \(m<n\), let
  \[
  d=\left\lfloor\frac m q\right\rfloor,
  \qquad r=m\bmod q;
  \]
- if \(m=n\), let
  \[
  d=2^k-1,
  \qquad r=q.
  \]

In both cases,
\[
m=dq+r. \tag{5}
\]
For \(m<n\), this is the division algorithm. For \(m=n\), it follows from
\[
(2^k-1)q+q=2^kq=n.
\]

We also have the bounds
\[
d<2^k \tag{6}
\]
and
\[
r<2^{k+1}. \tag{7}
\]
For \(m<n=2^kq\), division by the positive number \(q\) gives \(d<2^k\), while \(r<q=2^{k+1}-1<2^{k+1}\). At the endpoint, \(d=2^k-1<2^k\) and \(r=q=2^{k+1}-1<2^{k+1}\).

By the binary subset-sum result applied to (6), there is a subset
\[
I\subseteq\{1,2,4,\ldots,2^{k-1}\}
\]
whose elements sum to \(d\). Multiplying every selected element by \(q\) gives a subset
\[
I_q\subseteq B
\]
whose sum is \(dq\). The multiplication does not identify two selected elements because \(q>0\).

Similarly, by (7), there is a subset
\[
J\subseteq\{1,2,4,\ldots,2^k\}=A
\]
whose elements sum to \(r\).

Because \(A\) and \(B\) are disjoint, the union \(J\cup I_q\) consists of distinct proper divisors, and its sum is
\[
\sum_{x\in J}x+\sum_{x\in I_q}x=r+dq=m
\]
by (5). Thus every \(m\in\{0,1,\ldots,n\}\) belongs to \(\mathcal S(n)\). We have established
\[
\{0,1,\ldots,n\}\subseteq\mathcal S(n). \tag{8}
\]

### 5. No subset sum exceeds \(n\)

Conversely, take any subset \(T\subseteq D(n)\). All proper divisors are nonnegative, so
\[
\sum_{d\in T}d\le \sum_{d\in D(n)}d.
\]
Since \(n\) is perfect, the sum on the right is exactly \(n\). Therefore every subset sum lies between \(0\) and \(n\), and hence
\[
\mathcal S(n)\subseteq\{0,1,\ldots,n\}. \tag{9}
\]

Combining (8) and (9),
\[
\mathcal S(n)=\{0,1,\ldots,n\}.
\]
This set has \(n+1\) distinct elements. The sequence definition subtracts the one value \(0\), which comes from the empty subset, so
\[
a(n)=|\mathcal S(n)|-1=(n+1)-1=n.
\]
Therefore, for every even perfect number \(n\), \(a(n)=n\), as claimed.
